 What a Democratic sweep could mean for stocks — and why history says not much
 Jared Blikre Tue, November 3, 2026 at 12:26 PM EST 3 min read POLA.PVT 
 ^GSPC +0.36% 
 Polls and prediction markets have spent weeks pointing to a Democratic sweep. History says the outcome has shaped stocks for about three months, then barely at all. 
 That may surprise anyone bracing for a long night of maps and swing counties. Polymarket gave Democrats a 76% chance of winning both the House and the Senate as of Tuesday morning, with a Democratic House and a Republican Senate a distant second at 19%. 
 The House looks like the surer bet. The Senate is where the drama is. Republicans hold it 53-47, Democrats need a net gain of four seats, and polling models and prediction markets differ more on that chamber . Some races may not be called Tuesday night. 
 Stocks have seen this movie before. 
 Polymarket, Yahoo Finance Since 1946, midterms under a Republican president have ended three of the four ways Congress can go. A year later, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) was up an average of 15% to 16% after each one, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from the Election Day close. Over the long run, Wall Street's verdict has been bipartisan. 
 The short run is a different story. After the seven midterms that left Democrats running Congress, stocks rose an average of 11% over the next three months and were higher every time. After the lone Republican hold, in 2002, stocks fell 8% as the US moved toward war with Iraq. By the end of each president's term, all three outcomes were up on average. 
 Small samples, big caveats 
 None of this carries much statistical muscle. A Democratic sweep has happened seven times under a Republican president, a Democratic House with a Republican Senate twice, and a Republican hold once. A Republican House with a Democratic Senate has never happened. 
 Even the sweep record needs a footnote. In five of those seven years, Democrats already ran Congress. Only twice did a Republican president lose both chambers, as Democrats are trying to make happen this year — in 1954 under Dwight Eisenhower and in 2006 under George W. Bush. Stocks rose about 33% and 7% over the following year. 
 And the ride can get bumpy. The last time President Trump lost the House, in 2018, the S&P 500 sank nearly 15% by Christmas Eve as the Federal Reserve raised rates and trade tensions with China escalated. Then it bounced, finishing about 12% higher a year after the midterm election. The 2006 sweep by Democrats ran into the financial crisis, leaving stocks down about 38% by the time Bush left office in 2009. 
 Why the winner hasn't moved stocks much 
 Blue, red or divided, the S&P 500 was higher a year after all 20 midterms since 1946, measured from Election Day, with an average gain of about 14%. The closest call was 1946 itself, a gain of just 0.1%. The streak lines up with the strongest stretch of the presidential cycle , which runs from late in a midterm year into the next. 
 Story Continues Yahoo Finance So why doesn't the fight for Congress move markets more? Even a Democratic sweep would leave Washington divided, and the White House keeps many of the levers that move markets, like tariffs and war powers. 
 "We expect the 2026 midterm elections to yield a divided government, with sweeping policy changes constrained by Senate rules, party divisions, presidential veto power, and already wide federal deficits," Kurt Reiman, head of fixed income at UBS's Chief Investment Office, wrote in a recent report. 
 Or, as Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Global Advisors, put it in an August note, "Midterms are less about choosing a president than checking one."
